prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not attribute the new right-hand rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity to essential tremor or to cervical spondylosis
Do not stop propranolol abruptly: the postural tremor persists and abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with right-hand rest tremor and rigidity, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; rest tremor of a limb is the one supportive criterion (dream enactment is not one; the self-reported smell loss is one only on a validated test, UPSIT 27/40 with moderate microsmia when tested, which makes it clinically established), superimposed on or replacing the earlier essential tremor label; the response to levodopa may add a supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months; if a dopamine agonist is used instead or added, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness and ask about them at every visit [NICE_NG71]

Continue propranolol for the postural tremor, which levodopa does not treat, and measure lying and standing blood pressure and heart rate as levodopa is introduced, because propranolol blunts the heart-rate response to an orthostatic fall
Address the dream enactment: advise bedroom safety (protect his wife, remove sharp objects, padding beside the bed) and consider melatonin if episodes are injurious or frequent

Continue sertraline and review mood at each visit; treat constipation with fluids, fibre and an osmotic laxative such as macrogol; refer to physiotherapy for gait and balance and encourage a return to regular exercise [NICE_NG71]

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

interactions: Propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) blunts the compensatory heart-rate rise on standing and lowers blood pressure; levodopa can lower standing pressure further. Measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Sertraline with an MAO-B inhibitor: serotonin syndrome is rare; use the lowest dose and monitor. Fluoxetine and fluvoxamine are best avoided with rasagiline.
Atorvastatin and cholecalciferol: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
warnings: No dopamine-blocking drug on the current list.
Resting heart rate 58/min on propranolol: a further rate-lowering drug would add to bradycardia.
Sulfonamide allergy recorded: not relevant to levodopa, MAO-B inhibitors or dopamine agonists.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Rajesh Subramanian is a 62-year-old right-handed man presenting to the neurology outpatient clinic with a two-year history of progressive tremor and clumsiness primarily affecting his right hand. He was initially diagnosed with essential tremor by his primary care physician three years ago when he noticed intermittent shaking of both hands, predominantly while holding objects and during purposeful movements. He was started on propranolol 40 mg twice daily, which initially provided partial relief. However, over the past two years he has developed a new type of tremor in his right hand that occurs primarily at rest and seems to briefly worsen when he is anxious or distracted. He reports that his handwriting has become progressively smaller and more illegible over the past 18 months, which he initially attributed to spending too many hours typing at his computer. His wife has commented that his right hand seems clumsy during meals: he occasionally drops his fork and has difficulty cutting food. He has also noticed a general slowness in his movements, particularly in the mornings, describing it as a sensation of stiffness that takes time to loosen up. Over the past eight months he has stopped jogging because he feels unsteady and his right leg seems to drag slightly. His wife has noted that he walks more slowly and no longer swings his right arm naturally. She also reports that his facial expressions have become less animated, and he speaks more softly than he used to. The patient reports increasingly vivid dreams over the past year, and his wife describes episodes two to three times per month where he shouts and makes punching motions during sleep. He has experienced gradual onset constipation over the past three years requiring occasional use of stool softeners, and he has noticed a diminished sense of smell that he attributes to aging. He developed depression two years ago which was managed with sertraline. He has not noticed any cognitive decline aside from occasional word-finding difficulty. He denies visual hallucinations, dysphagia, urinary symptoms, or postural dizziness. He has a history of cervical spondylosis identified on imaging four years ago during evaluation for neck stiffness. He is concerned because his paternal uncle was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in his 70s.

Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly narrow-based gait with reduced right arm swing. Stride length mildly shortened on the right. No festination or freezing. Mild difficulty with tandem walking. Pull test: takes 2 corrective steps before stabilizing. Able to rise from chair without arm assistance but slowly. No circumduction or foot drop.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 26/30, losing points on trail-making (1), delayed recall (2), and clock drawing (1). Speech is mildly hypophonic with reduced prosody but fluent, comprehension and repetition intact. No aphasia or neglect.
neurological_exam.motor: No muscle wasting or fasciculations. Moderate cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and mild cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist. Bradykinesia demonstrated on finger tapping: the right hand shows progressive decrement in amplitude and speed; the left hand shows mild slowing. Strength 5/5 in bilateral deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger flexors and abductors, hip flexors, quadriceps, hamstrings, and ankle dorsiflexors. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
